These planktonic paralarvae immediately commence active feeding on copepods and other small zooplankton, beginning a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through several ontogenetic stages. Field sampling indicates that the transition to a reproductively active adult is marked by the attainment of a mantle length at puberty of 7.0 cm [Lp = 7.0 cm], a threshold that corresponds with the onset of gonadal development and the differentiation of the reproductive tract. Interestingly, this species exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females growing considerably larger than males before reaching senescence. Female Cranchia scabra experience natural mortality after a single, semelparous reproductive event, with the maximum mantle length at death for females recorded at 15.0 cm [Li = 15.0 cm]. This terminal size is considerably larger than the size at maturity, reflecting a substantial post-pubertal growth phase during which somatic tissues continue to expand even as reproductive structures develop. Correspondingly, the wet weight at death for a female reaching this asymptotic mantle length is estimated at 82.7 g [Wwi = 82.7 g], a mass that is consistent with the cubic relationship between mantle length and body volume observed in teuthoid squids. Growth trajectories reconstructed from statolith increment analysis reveal that Cranchia scabra paralarvae attain a mantle length at birth of 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm] and then undergo an exponential increase in body dimensions during the first few months of life. Puberty, defined by the onset of spermatophore production in males and ovulation in females, is reached when individuals achieve a mantle length at puberty of 7.0 cm [Lp = 7.0 cm], a developmental milestone that occurs several weeks prior to the terminal size. The substantial difference between the size at maturity and the final maximum mantle length at death for females of 15.0 cm [Li = 15.0 cm] indicates that post-pubertal growth continues at a moderate pace, allowing females to store additional energy reserves for the demanding spawning migration and egg deposition process. This decoupling of reproductive maturation from somatic growth cessation is a common feature among oegopsid squids and likely reflects selective pressures for increased fecundity through larger body size at the time of spawning.

Allometric scaling relationships derived from midwater trawl collections indicate that a female Cranchia scabra with a mantle length of 10.2 cm exhibits a wet weight of approximately 26 g, and applying the cube-law to the terminal size yields a calculated wet weight at death of 82.7 g [Wwi = 82.7 g] for a female reaching 15.0 cm [Li = 15.0 cm] mantle length. This mass represents the culmination of a growth period lasting roughly one year under the prevailing thermal regime of the species’ habitat. The gonadosomatic index of 15% [GSI = 15%] was measured at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The combination of a short life span for females of 365.0 days [am = 365.0 days] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a moderate size at puberty, and a large terminal body size reinforces the interpretation of Cranchia scabra as a capital breeder that accumulates resources during its juvenile and subadult phases to fuel a single, high-investment reproductive bout.
